tbpn_example.episode_title: Crypto Day (Brian Armstrong, Balaji, Chris Dixon, Katie Haun and more)

notes: Research: 5 Whys originates with Sakichi Toyoda and was made the core problem-solving discipline of the Toyota Production System by Taiichi Ohno (Toyota Production System: Beyond Large-Scale Production, 1988). Classic case chosen: Ohno's own machine-stop chain (fuse blew / bearing under-lubricated / pump not pumping / shaft worn / no strainer, metal scrap got in). Design decision: keep exactly the registry's four slots (problem, why, root_cause, countermeasure) and its two relations (because, addressed_by); recurrence evidence goes in the problem slot and stated systemic conditions go in the why slot at deeper levels, rather than adding an evidence slot, so the framework stays comparable with its siblings. Scout returned three candidates: (1) Brian Armstrong's first-person post-mortem of the Coinbase support-bribery breach, six stated causal layers; (2) the AWS us-east-1 DynamoDB DNS outage, five layers but mostly hosts reading a WSJ write-up; (3) the Nate 'AI' shopping app fraud, five layers. Chose (1): the deepest stated chain in the corpus, told by the person who owns the system, and its deep layers are systemic (outsourced 24/7 staffing, bribe-versus-wage economics, vendor perimeter, scope-limiting controls) rather than blame on the bribed agents, which is exactly the framework's point. Decisions: idea_bearing_slot is countermeasure, not root_cause, because in 5 Whys the opportunity is the fix that reaches the systemic layer, and all three idea fields sit on derived countermeasure nodes (c4, c5, c6). Slot countermeasure's typical_provenance is refined from the registry's 'derived' to 'either': both examples contain stated shallow countermeasures (fuse replacement, relocation, bounty, AI support) alongside the derived one that reaches the root cause, and that contrast is the framework's teaching point. Validate: 0 errors, 0 warnings.
